doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: West Babylon band and the director's silent looks
summary: He describes his small, inclusive high school band and how his director looked at him to signal mistakes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: They didn’t work on it first of all, hard enough, because they may be first trumpet in some orchestra and somebody asked them to make a recording of it and they could play it, physically they were fine trumpet players. But the most important thing, and that’s another reason why I used the books that I could teach them this, to the band directors and to the people who were going to be professional trumpet players. See because it’s the same. You’re teaching music. You know? They have to be musically strong and then you don’t have to have a band director that plays the trumpet to learn to play the trumpet right. He taught the flute players, my band director. He taught the saxophone players. They all were good musicians. We had about 50 people in our band usually, because it was a small school. West Babylon was a tiny little part of Babylon but it was a little, own separate school district. And we only had 50 people in the band. You know our marching band was in the smallest category and stuff. And about every year about ten percent of that band went into music. Like the thing with Glenn Drewes and me, okay, if either of us, the band director would conduct here and the trumpets were sitting over here right next to him. He’d be conducting away you know, and the band was sounding just as

average as it always did. And then he’d look at us and never stop the band. And I’d say, “Glen, I think we did something wrong.” Because that’s all he would do. He’d never call us out in band. But you know people couldn’t play the same part — he never said anything to them because he knew why they were in band. So it became a really inclusive band. We were all close. The ones that played well and the ones that didn’t. And then I’d go home I’d say, “Mom, he looked at me today.” She knew what that meant. You know what I’m saying? Because he knew that I was going to take that music home and I was going to dissect the section he looked at us at and I was going to try to find what he — see that was the point. See I didn’t know what he was looking for. So I was looking. He didn’t say you know you missed that lick there. No. He didn’t tell me what was wrong. I didn’t know if it was an articulation, maybe I was missing an accidental or something. Usually not, because I played by ear mostly you know. I just knew what fit in and what didn’t. But you know or some rhythm wasn’t exactly right. And I’d come back the next day and I’d go okay I’m going to see if he’s going to look at me in that spot. I mean it was like a game for him. He knew. He had everybody’s number. See he had it all in numbers. This kid didn’t want to go to band because he didn’t want to go to study hall because he’d get beat up. He might be a little, like a little meek person. That’s what went on in those days. There were a lot of bullies.
